Title: FBM KLCI opens higher on bargain-hunting, resilient domestic fundamental
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Bursa Malaysia opened higher on Wednesday, maintaining a cautious but positive tone, supported by continued bargain-hunting activities and resilient domestic fundamentals.
At 9.10am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) gained 4.50 points, or 0.27 per cent, to 1,627.85 from yesterday's close of 1,623.35. The index opened 0.59 points firmer at 1,623.94.
Across the broader market, losers outnumbered gainers 193 to 137, while 291 counters were unchanged, 2,234 were untraded, and 21 were suspended.
Turnover stood at 239.44 million units worth RM140.08 million.

Title: Dollar languishes as focus turns to CPI, Fed speakers
Article:
TOKYO:The dollar languished on Wednesday as traders awaited fresh signals on the timing of interest rate hikes to contend with persistent inflation.
The greenback weakened from an 18-month high in the previous session as oil prices eased and investors reassessed the AI-fuelled rally that has supported demand for US assets.
The euro clung to gains as budget concerns in France kept regional bond yields elevated and markets on edge.
Attention now focuses on the release of US consumer price index data as well as speeches from Federal Reserve policymakers that could clarify the outlook for interest rates.
"The risk is the core CPI surprises to the upside because of strong consumer demand and higher costs, pushing up market pricing of an October Fed hike and the USD," Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said in a note.
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, edged 0.02 per cent lower to 102.16, following a 0.35 per cent slide on Tuesday. The euro rose 0.04 per cent to US$1.1203.
The yen was little changed at 158.32 per dollar, and sterling rose 0.03 per cent to US$1.3256.
The dollar extended losses on Tuesday after New York Fed President John Williams said he still expects one more rate hike this year, but sees no need for further increases in 2027.
The US Labor Department is due to release its CPI for September, which is expected to have risen 0.60 per cent month-on-month after increasing 0.40 per cent in August, while annual inflation is seen accelerating to 3.60 per cent from 3.40 per cent. Additionally, the Fed is due to publish its Beige Book.
Traders see a 77 per cent chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 51 per cent a month ago, while pricing in about 75 basis points of tightening by late 2027, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed.
Investors abandoned bets on a Fed rate hike later this month after two policymakers argued for gathering more evidence before deciding whether further tightening is needed, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller said inflation expectations remained "well anchored".
Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin is scheduled to participate in a fireside chat in Virginia, while Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman is set to take part in talks in Bangkok.
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank's annual meetings continue in Bangkok, with several appearances expected by European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde on Wednesday.
The Australian dollar strengthened 0.06 per cent against the greenback to US$0.6984, while New Zealand's kiwi strengthened 0.09 per cent to US$0.5614.

Title: Perak to prioritise local water needs before supplying Penang - Exco
Article:
IPOH: The Perak state government has assured that the state's domestic, industrial and agricultural water needs will be prioritised before any surplus is supplied to Penang under the Bulk Water Supply Agreement (BWSA).
Perak Infrastructure, Energy, Water and Transport Committee chairman Datuk Seri Mohammad Nizar Jamaluddin said the approach was crucial to ensuring a sustainable water supply in the state, particularly in anticipation of rising demand in the years ahead.
"Whether for domestic consumption, industrial use or padI cultivation, we will prioritise Perak's water needs, with demand estimated at 1,500 million litres per day.
"We will consider supplying water to Penang only if there is a surplus after meeting Perak's domestic, industrial and agricultural requirements," he told Bernama.
He was commenting on Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's announcement during the tabling of Budget 2027 that the Madani government had facilitated a 40-year BWSA between the Perak and Penang state governments.
The agreement, signed between Khazanah Air Perak Sdn Bhd (KAP) and Penang Water Supply Corporation (PBAPP), targets the initial delivery of treated water in the first quarter of 2032.
Nizar said the project would also support the development of the Kerian Integrated Green Industrial Park (KIGIP), which is emerging as a key destination for new investments, particularly in the digital sector.
"KIGIP is benefiting from the spillover of the digital industry from Penang. The assurance of a reliable water supply will give investors greater confidence to establish and expand their businesses in Perak," he said.
He added that a stable water supply would also help address supply disruptions in the Kamunting industrial area and at Tasik Bukit Merah in Kerian, an important water source for agricultural and domestic use.
The large-scale project would also generate additional revenue for KAP, create job opportunities and enable more systematic management of water levels at Tasik Bukit Merah, he said.
"Local communities, particularly padifarmers and inland fishermen around Tasik Bukit Merah, will also benefit from better management of the lake's water levels, which could help reduce the risk of drought," he said.

Title: Oil prices climb as traders weigh Saudi supply risk, Russian diesel flow
Article:
TOKYO:Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as traders weighed supply risks from fighting between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and Saudi Arabia against the prospect of increased diesel exports from Russia.
Brent crude futures rose 89 cents, or eight-tenths of a per cent, to US$106.58 a barrel by 0030 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 80 cents, or nine-tenths of a per cent, to US$94.94. Brent fell 0.9 per cent on Tuesday, while WTI rose 0.4 per cent.
"Supply concern stemming from conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is driving prices higher," said chief strategist Hiroyuki Kikukawa at Nissan Securities Investment, a unit of Nissan Securities.
"However, the expectation that increased Russian diesel exports will ease market tightness is likely to limit sharp price movement in either direction," Kikukawa said, projecting WTI to trade between US$90 and US$100 a barrel.
The Houthis attacked an administrative building belonging to state-owned oil firm Saudi Aramco in the city of Dhahran, causing a limited fire, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said on Wednesday.
The group has fired ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia over the past week in retaliation for the kingdom's support of Yemeni government forces. Riyadh's international airport has been hit four times, with a strike on Saturday killing 13 people.
Last month, Saudi Arabia raised oil production despite disruption to shipments caused by the US-Iran war, leading to a sharp production increase from OPEC+ — the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and partners, including Russia — OPEC said on Tuesday.
Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz to keep oil prices high and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
In Russia, the government said on Tuesday it did not see any direct link between peace talks with Ukraine and its deal to export diesel to the US.
The comment came after Reuters reported that US envoys had told Ukrainian officials on Friday that the deal was part of an attempt to draw Russia back to negotiations for a peace settlement.

Title: 4,289 bullying cases recorded in schools from March to August, says Fadhlina
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: An average of 24 bullying cases were recorded daily in schools between March and August this year, bringing the total to 4,289 cases over six months.
Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said the cases, including incidents in hostels, comprised 2,480 involving physical bullying, 1,386 verbal bullying, 243 non-verbal bullying and 180 cyberbullying.
In response, she said, the Education Ministry has stepped up hostel monitoring through expanded closed-circuit television (CCTV) coverage, additional assistant wardens and safety audits.
CCTV cameras were installed in 200 boarding schools in 2025 and another 333 schools this year, with allocations of RM3 million and RM5 million respectively.
Another RM15 million has been allocated for 2027 to expand CCTV coverage to 1,000 schools nationwide.
Fadhlina said 300 MyStep Hostel Assistant Warden Personnel (MyPWA) had been deployed since April to support more than 10,000 existing wardens, particularly in strengthening night-time supervision.
The ministry had also audited hostel safety at 850 schools, with follow-up efforts this year through the Student Safety and Well-being Survey (TKKM) and In-Situ Guidance: Student Safety and Well-being (BKKM).
"Safety monitoring cannot rely solely on physical facilities.
"Supervision by school personnel, awareness of changes in students' behaviour and prompt action on complaints are also important components in ensuring a safe hostel environment," she said in a parliamentary reply.
Fadhlina said the ministry had upgraded its Bullying Complaints Portal to allow anonymous reports, giving students and witnesses a safer channel to lodge complaints.
Bullying cases are managed under the ministry's Circular No. 12 of 2023, while school safety is guided by Circular No. 3 of 2026.
The Anti-Bullying Act 2026, drafted with the Legal Affairs Division, came into force in stages from March 1 and was fully implemented on June 16. It provides for an Anti-Bullying Tribunal through which victims can seek redress.
"The ministry continues to strengthen its comprehensive approach to tackling bullying, covering enforcement, monitoring of school and hostel environments, victim protection, psychosocial intervention and student character development," she said.
Prevention efforts also include the School Anti-Bullying Framework for Empowerment (SAFE), introduced under Budget 2026, which promotes caring school practices, peer support and targeted counselling.
Fadhlina was responding to Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh), who asked about the number of bullying cases since the Anti-Bullying Act 2026 came into force and improvements to hostel monitoring following revelations during the inquest into Zara Qairina's death.

Title: [UPDATED] Police to send team to Japan after five Malaysians arrested over 5kg cocaine hidden in shoe insoles
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Police will send an investigation team to Japan following the arrest of five Malaysians after 5kg of cocaine was found hidden in their shoe insoles at Haneda Airport in Tokyo on Oct 10.
Federal Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said the team would gather information about the arrests, including details of local and international drug syndicate networks.
He said Japanese authorities were also investigating the source of the cocaine and working to identify syndicate members and international drug trafficking networks.
"Japanese authorities have informed NCID about the arrest of two Malaysian men and three women at Haneda Airport on Oct 10.
"Their customs officers found 5kg of cocaine hidden in the insoles of shoes worn by all five suspects," he said in a statement.
The confirmation clarifies earlier reports that four men and one woman had been arrested in the case.
Hussein said checks on travel records showed that six Malaysians had departed together from Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 2 for Haneda on Oct 9 for a holiday.
However, only five were detained by Japanese authorities, while the sixth was not arrested and has since returned to Malaysia.
He said NCID had identified all six people, aged between 19 and 26, including the person who had returned to Malaysia.
"Five of them are from Sarawak, and checks showed that none had any previous criminal record," he said.
Hussein advised the public to be wary of holiday offers, particularly those involving requests to carry other people's bags or belongings overseas.
He also urged the public not to accept or carry items without knowing their contents, to avoid being exploited as drug mules.
Anyone with information on drug-related activities can contact the NCID hotline at 012-208 7222.
Japanese media had earlier reported that five Malaysians were arrested after customs officers found
cocaine concealed in shoe insoles
when they arrived at Haneda Airport.
According to TBS News DIG, each suspect was believed to have been carrying about 1kg of cocaine, with two 500g packages concealed in each shoe.
The report also quoted a suspect as saying that he had been offered payment of RM8,000 per person to transport drugs overseas through the Telegram messaging app.
Japanese media estimated the total value of the seized cocaine around 120 million yen (RM3.1 million).
Meanwhile, Tokyo Reporter, citing a Nippon News Network (NNN) report on Oct 12, claimed that one of the five Malaysians arrested had been detained alongside his wife and several friends.
However, the police have yet to confirm whether two of the suspects are married.

Title: 27 stations record unhealthy API readings across Peninsular Malaysia
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 27 air quality monitoring stations nationwide recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as of 8am today, all in Peninsular Malaysia.
According to the Department of Environment's (DoE) Air Pollutant Index Management System, Pasir Gudang in Johor recorded the highest reading at 177.
Nilai in Negri Sembilan followed at 174, while Klang and Johan Setia in Selangor each recorded 173.
In Melaka, Bukit Rambai recorded an API reading of 169, followed by Bandaraya Melaka at 164 and Alor Gajah at 156.
In the Klang Valley, Cheras recorded 168 and Batu Muda 164 in Kuala Lumpur, while Putrajaya registered 165.
Other areas in Selangor with unhealthy readings were Banting (160), Shah Alam (159) and Petaling Jaya (154).
In Johor, Kota Tinggi recorded 166, followed by Larkin (164), Pengerang (162) and Batu Pahat (154). Port Dickson and Seremban in Negri Sembilan recorded readings of 165 and 160 respectively.
On the east coast, Kemaman and Paka in Terengganu recorded readings of 156 and 155 respectively, while Indera Mahkota in Kuantan registered 155 and Rompin 153 in Pahang.
Sabah and Sarawak recorded moderate air quality, with Sandakan registering 95 and Samarahan 94. Kuala Terengganu recorded the highest moderate reading nationwide at 97.
Langkawi in Kedah was the only monitoring station to record good air quality, with a reading of 40.
No monitoring stations recorded very unhealthy or hazardous air quality.
An API reading of 0 to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy and above 300 hazardous.

Title: Govt may allow refugees to fill labour gaps in 3D sectors
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The government may allow registered refugees to fill labour shortages in the 3D (dirty, dangerous and difficult) sectors to reduce Malaysia's dependence on foreign workers.
Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the proposal could be considered by examining data on about 225,000 people with refugee status, based on records maintained by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
He said the government intended to identify refugees of working age who had passed screening to assess their potential to meet the country's workforce needs.
"On the other hand, we have 225,000 people whom UNHCR recognises as refugees. They are right here in front of us. This is a big idea, but it has not been implemented yet.
"If we could compile data on these 225,000 people and identify those within the productive age range, such as 20, 25 or 30, who have been screened, we would have the data.
"Our intention is to meet workforce needs without necessarily recruiting from abroad.
"For example, if an oil palm plantation in Pasir Gudang needs 100 workers, there are two options. We could recruit workers from Bangladesh and pay all the associated costs, or check our existing refugee registration database.
"For now, I am not ruling out the possibility of taking this route to meet the actual workforce needs we face," he said in the Dewan Rakyat yesterday.
He was responding to Jimmy Puah Wee Tse (PH-Tebrau), who sought clarification on whether the government planned to allow Rohingya refugees registered under the Refugee Documentation Programme (DPP) to work in the 3D sectors, particularly amid a shortage of foreign workers.
Saifuddin said foreign worker requirements were currently concentrated in five economic sectors, namely manufacturing, plantations, agriculture, construction and services.
He said labour shortages in these sectors could affect economic activities, particularly jobs such as harvesting oil palm fresh fruit bunches and laying bricks.
"There are five economic sectors that require workers. The Economy Ministry has set a ceiling on the number of foreign workers who can be brought in.
"Under the 13th Malaysia Plan, the number must not exceed 10 per cent of the workforce. Our workforce stands at 17 million, meaning the ceiling is 1.7 million throughout the 13th Malaysia Plan for the five economic sectors.
"If these five sectors do not have foreign workers, our economy will be affected. That means there would be no one to harvest oil palm or lay bricks. That is the reality.
"Every year, the Home Ministry is among the regulatory agencies involved in decisions on approvals for foreign workers and related matters," he said.

Title: 'No caviar here': Sushi King wins Customs dispute
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: They may be tiny, colourful and look a little like caviar, but fish eggs found on sushi are not necessarily considered a luxury delicacy under the law.
The High Court has ruled that tobiko (flying fish roe), masago (capelin roe) and frozen mentaiko (pollock roe) imported by restaurant chain Sushi King Sdn Bhd are not caviar substitutes, despite being seasoned, coloured and preserved.
Judge Norliza Othman ruled this when dismissing an appeal by the Customs Department director-general against a Customs Appeal Tribunal decision in favour of Sushi King over the classification of the three products.
The dispute centred on whether the fish eggs should be classified as caviar substitutes, which attract an 8 per cent import duty, or other prepared or preserved fish, which carry zero import duty.
On Oct 8, 2020, Sushi King submitted three applications to the Customs Department seeking tariff rulings for the imported fish roe.
The department classified the products as caviar substitutes, which attract an 8 per cent import duty.
Dissatisfied with the classification, Sushi King sought a review and proposed different tariff codes for the three products. However, Customs maintained its decision on Dec 7, 2021.
Sushi King then appealed to the Customs Appeal Tribunal, which ruled in its favour on Dec 1, 2023, and set aside the department's classification.
This prompted the Customs Department director-general to challenge the tribunal's decision in the High Court.
In its appeal, Customs argued that the products qualified as caviar substitutes because they had undergone several processes, including cleaning, seasoning, colouring and freezing.
It maintained that the processing methods and fish egg content met the requirements for caviar substitutes under the Customs Duties Order 2017.
Customs also argued that how the products were consumed should not determine whether they qualified as caviar substitutes.
However, Sushi King maintained that the products were commonly used as toppings or garnishes in Japanese cuisine and were neither consumed nor marketed as alternatives to caviar.
The company argued that not all processed or seasoned fish eggs could automatically be classified as caviar substitutes.
In her judgment, Norliza agreed with Sushi King, saying that not all fish eggs could be considered caviar substitutes and that how they were consumed was an important factor in determining their classification.
"Fish roe is a wide, all-encompassing term used to describe fish eggs, but not all fish roe is caviar or a caviar substitute.
"In this regard, caviar substitute is a very specific subset of fish roe based on its origin, methods of consumption and method of processing, which aims to mimic sturgeon caviar," she said in her grounds of judgment published by the Judiciary Department yesterday.
Norliza said Sushi King's imported products were used as toppings or garnishes in Japanese cuisine rather than being marketed as alternatives to caviar.
She said the World Customs Organisation's explanatory notes described caviar substitutes as products made from the eggs of fish other than sturgeon, which were prepared and consumed as caviar.
The judge said imported goods must be classified according to the relevant legal provisions and the WCO's guidelines.
She also found that the Customs Appeal Tribunal had carefully examined the products, including their composition, preparation methods and how they were consumed, before ruling in Sushi King's favour.
Senior federal counsel Nur Aishah Maulat Ahmad Zakiuddin and federal counsel Muhaimin Mohamed represented the appellant, while S. Saravana Kumar and Darshini Sharma appeared for Sushi King.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Creating a senior-friendly tourism ecosystem
Article:
LETTER:
At what age is someone officially considered as a senior citizen - 55, 60, 62 or 65? The answer depends on where you are and what you are paying for.
Malaysia's National Policy for Older Persons defines an older person as someone aged 60 and above. Yet the tourism and leisure businesses do not apply the same threshold consistently.
Golden Screen Cinemas, for example, offers senior citizen rates to patrons aged 55 years old and above. Penang Hill and Sunway Lagoon use 60, while Petrosains places senior admission at 61 and above.
The differences are not unique to Malaysia. In the United States, the National Park Service offers its Senior Pass from 62 years old, while English Heritage in Britain provides senior concession tickets from 65.
So there is clearly no universal age at which a tourist suddenly becomes "senior".
Chronological age alone does not tell us about whether a person is healthy, active, financially independent or physically restricted.
This matters as Malaysia's population ages. People in their late 55s or early 60s today may be very different from someone of the same age several decades ago.
Many continue working, travelling and participating actively in leisure. Others may experience mobility, health or financial constraints earlier.
Should Malaysia therefore lower all senior discounts to 55? Not necessarily.
A blanket rule could increase costs for attractions and reduce ticket revenue, particularly for operators already providing substantial concessions. Age alone also does not indicate financial need.
But, the current situation deserves another look. Instead of requiring every attraction to adopt the same age, the tourism industry could distinguish between an official senior citizen entitlement and a senior tourism market.
The official threshold of 60 could remain for government related concessions.
Tourism businesses, however, could have the flexibility to recognise the broader 55 plus market through off peak discounts, weekday promotions, loyalty programmes or special packages.
This could benefit both sides. Senior tourists may be encouraged to travel more frequently, while attractions could attract visitors during quieter periods.
They may also benefit from spending on food, retail, transport and family members travelling together.
More importantly, senior friendly tourism should not end with a cheaper ticket.
Accessible toilets, seating areas, safe walkways, clear information, simple digital booking and helpful staff may matter far more than saving a few ringgit.
Malaysia therefore does not necessarily need one compulsory age for every senior discount but greater clarity over what "senior" means, why a concession is being offered and whom it is intended to help.
LIEW SIEN LEONG
Lecturer
School of Tourism, Hospitality and Event Management
Universiti Utara Malaysia
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Ringgit opens marginally higher against US dollar on weaker DXY
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit opened marginally higher against the US dollar on Wednesday, supported by a weaker US Dollar Index (DXY) as investors reassessed the outlook for US interest rates following signals that the Federal Reserve may adopt a less aggressive monetary policy stance.
At 8am, the ringgit rose to 4.0830/0880 against the greenback from Tuesday's close of 4.0835/0880.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the DXY fell 0.40 per cent to 102.810 points after US Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams indicated that the Fed Funds Rate may not be raised in 2027, as inflation is expected to ease gradually towards the two per cent target.
"In addition, Williams suggested that the US economy is not overheating and therefore, it does not warrant an aggressive rate increase," he told Bernama.
Meanwhile, Mohd Afzanizam said US inflation numbers would be closely monitored, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) projected to rise to 3.6 per cent in September from 3.4 per cent previously, based on consensus estimates.
Therefore, he said it could be positive for the ringgit, although market sentiment remains cautious.
"Hence, the ringgit-US dollar could maintain its narrow range trade of RM4.07 to RM4.09 today," he added.
At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly lower against a basket of major currencies.
The local note was higher against the Japanese yen to 2.5790/5823 from 2.5833/5864 at Tuesday's close, but edged down against the British pound to 5.4128/4195 from 5.4057/4177 and eased against the euro to 4.5734/5790 from 4.5654/5704.
However, against its Asean peers, the ringgit traded mixed.
The local note advanced against the Thai baht to 12.1626/1848 from 12.1663/1844 at Tuesday's close, but was marginally lower against the Singapore dollar to 3.1903/1950 from 3.1902/1940 yesterday.
Meanwhile, the ringgit was unchanged against the Indonesian rupiah at 228.1/228.4, and remained flat against the Philippine peso at 6.50/6.51.

Title: Immigration identifies 224 hotspots linked to undocumented migrants
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Immigration Department has identified 224 hotspots nationwide linked to the presence and activities of foreigners, including illegal settlements and overcrowded rental houses.
Immigration director-general Datuk Zakaria Shaaban said other locations included workers' quarters at construction sites and business premises dominated by foreigners.
He said these locations required close attention and enforcement monitoring.
"From 2023 to June 15 this year, a total of 16,431 Op Sapu operations were conducted. These operations involved raids on various illegal settlements, including squatter houses, workers' quarters and lodging houses found to be occupied by undocumented migrants.
"During the period, 50,382 foreigners were detained for various offences under the Immigration Act," he said in an exclusive interview.
Zakaria said a location's status as a hotspot was not fixed but subject to ongoing assessment based on intelligence, public complaints, findings from enforcement operations and current analysis.
The assessment also took into account changes in the patterns of foreigners' presence, intelligence findings and enforcement action, he added.
"The department will continue to carry out targeted, intelligence-led enforcement while strengthening cooperation with local authorities and enforcement agencies within their respective jurisdictions.
"Action will also be taken against employers and other parties that employ or shelter undocumented migrants, or facilitate their presence, in accordance with the law," he said.
Zakaria said illegal settlements and villages involved the jurisdictions of several parties, including local authorities and other agencies.
"Within the department's jurisdiction, enforcement focuses on foreigners who are in the country in violation of immigration laws.
"As such, enforcement does not end once an operation has been carried out.
"Monitoring and enforcement will continue based on information, complaints and intelligence, including through strategic cooperation with local authorities and other enforcement agencies to address the presence of undocumented migrants at identified locations," he said.
He said the department also prioritised action against parties contributing to the presence of undocumented migrants, including employers who hired them or parties who sheltered them or allowed them to stay on their premises.
These included employers hiring undocumented migrants and parties sheltering them or allowing them to remain on their premises, subject to the provisions of the law in force.
"This approach is strengthened through intelligence, data analysis and information-sharing between agencies to identify high-risk locations and enable more targeted and sustained enforcement.
"Addressing this issue requires a comprehensive, inter-agency approach, not only through operations against undocumented migrants but also by tackling the factors that enable them to remain and work illegally in the country," he said.

Title: US high court to decide if cooking qualifies as terror support
Article:
WASHINGTON: Does cooking for members of a Nigerian separatist group amount to providing "material support" for terrorism?
That's the thorny question facing the conservative-majority US Supreme Court.
In a brief order Tuesday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Trump administration's bid to reinstate the ruling that denied asylum to a Nigerian man who was deported for having provided material support to a terrorist group.
The case will be considered during the Court's current term, which began Oct 5 and runs through late June.
Beyond Izuchukwu Ozurumba's case, the ruling could have far-reaching implications for asylum seekers, depending largely on how the nine justices – six conservatives and three liberals – interpret the concept of "material support."
Izuchukwu Ozurumba says he was forced to cook for about six months at a separatist group's camp in southern Nigeria beginning in 2022.
He then fled to Venezuela and from there crossed the US-Mexico border illegally in the summer of 2023.
In 2024, a US immigration judge denied Ozurumba's asylum claim and ordered him deported citing a provision of US immigration law that bars foreign nationals who provide "material support" to a terrorist organisation from receiving asylum.
The decision was later upheld on appeal.
Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in April 2025, according to his lawyers.
But a federal appeals court later overturned the earlier decisions and sent the case back to the immigration court for reconsideration.
"Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have 'sustained' the organization in the broadest possible sense...but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the appeals court wrote.
"As far as the record shows, Ozurumba was simply a captive labourer whose work had nothing to do with those activities."
The Trump administration, as part of its sweeping campaign of deportations of undocumented immigrants, is asking the Supreme Court to overturn the appeals court ruling.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Ali Baba licences, Gaza and troubled housing project among Dewan Rakyat's focus today
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Legislation to curb "Ali Baba" licensing practices, Malaysia's diplomatic efforts to sustain the Gaza ceasefire and the fate of a troubled housing project are among the key issues expected to be raised in the Dewan Rakyat today.
According to the Order Paper, Syahredzan Johan (PH-Bangi) will ask the Economy Minister about the progress of drafting the Anti-Rent-Seeking Act and the timeline for its tabling in Parliament to curb Ali Baba licensing practices.
The conflict in West Asia is also expected to feature prominently, with Ahmad Tarmizi Sulaiman (PN-Sik) seeking an update from the Foreign Minister on Malaysia's diplomatic efforts at the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation to ensure the Gaza ceasefire holds and humanitarian aid continues to reach the territory.
The fate of 1,120 residential units at the abandoned Residensi Wilayah Salak Selatan apartment project is another key issue, with Fong Kui Lun (PH-Bukit Bintang) asking the Housing and Local Government Ministry to explain its rescue plan, including a proposal to appoint a rescue developer if the Scheme of Arrangement fails.
Jimmy Puah (PH-Tebrau) will raise preparations for workforce transition plans in response to the challenges posed by artificial intelligence, while Suhaizan Kaiat (PH-Pulai) will ask about median wages and graduate underemployment, particularly those working in jobs below their qualifications.
Other matters on the agenda include the future direction of Tabung Pahlawan, with Nordin Ahmad Ismail (PN-Lumut) seeking an explanation from the Defence Minister on its transformation; aid distribution to Sekolah Agama Rakyat in 2026, raised by Datuk Ahmad Saad @ Yahaya (PN-Pokok Sena); and agricultural input costs and bushfires on Pulau Bruit, Sarawak, raised by Sabri Azit (PN-Jerai).
After the question-and-answer session, the Dewan Rakyat will consider a motion by the prime minister to appoint members of parliament to the Parliamentary Services Council.
Under the motion, two government MPs, Ramkarpal Singh (PH-Bukit Gelugor) and Datuk Seri Hasni Mohammad (BN-Simpang Renggam), and two opposition MPs, Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran) and Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu), will be nominated to the council under Section 3(2)(f) of the Parliamentary Services Act 2025.
The Dewan Rakyat will then resume debate on the 2027 Supply Bill at the policy stage, following the tabling of the 2027 Budget by Prime Minister and Finance Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last Friday.
According to the calendar for the Third Meeting of the Fifth Session of the 15th Parliament, the policy-stage debate on Budget 2027 runs from Oct 12 to 22, followed by four days of ministerial winding-up speeches beginning Oct 26.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting is scheduled to run for 37 days, until Dec 8.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Singapore central bank keeps monetary policy unchanged
Article:
SINGAPORE: Singapore's central bank on Wednesday kept its monetary policy settings unchanged.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it would maintain the prevailing rate of appreciation in its exchange rate-based policy band, known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, or S$NEER.
There would be no change to the width of the policy band or the level at which it is centred, it said.
All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected the MAS to tighten monetary policy.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Gold subdued ahead of US inflation data, Warsh remarks
Article:
NEW YORK: Gold prices edged lower on Tuesday, while investors awaited key US inflation data and remarks from the Federal Reserve chair due later this week to gauge the outlook on monetary policy.
Spot gold fell 0.3 per cent to US$4,157.90 per ounce by 2.15pm EDT (1815 GMT). US gold futures for December settled down 0.3 per cent at US$4,177.30 per ounce.
"We have some inflation data that's coming out later this week. So market is kind of waiting to see how that plays out," said Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX.
He noted the Fed chairman will deliver his last speech before the upcoming rate meeting on Thursday, and anticipates a quieter session ahead of Wednesday's and Thursday's events.
Investors are looking ahead to the Consumer Price Index data on Wednesday, while Thursday's Producer Price Index figures and remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will be closely parsed.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller on Tuesday said the recent rise in US bond yields reflects stronger economic growth rather than higher inflation expectations, which remain "well anchored".
Gold loses its appeal in a high-interest-rate environment as it does not yield interest.
Currently, traders see only a 19 per cent chance of a Fed rate hike this month but are pricing in an 88 per cent chance of a December increase, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Meanwhile, oil prices fell on Tuesday and were on track for their first decline in nearly a week.
The dollar and benchmark 10-year Treasury yields slipped from their respective highs, but still hovered near elevated levels.
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday highlighted risks from elevated public debt levels and rising bond yields that may be driven higher still by war-driven inflation pressures.
"Interest rate hikes have increasingly become a double-edged sword for gold. While higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as gold, they also intensify the fiscal burden on many governments and thereby exacerbate debt sustainability concerns," analysts at Commerzbank said in a note.
Elsewhere, spot silver fell 1.8 per cent to US$59.25 per ounce, platinum edged 1.4 per cent lower to US$1,661.18 per ounce and palladium dropped 1.5 per cent to US$1,126.95 per ounce.

Title: US stocks dip ahead of inflation data as tech sell-off hits Asia
Article:
NEW YORK: Wall Street stocks were mostly lower at the end of a choppy session Tuesday, digesting solid results from US banks and a pullback in Asian markets prompted by worries over the AI investment boom.
While JPMorgan Chase missed analyst estimates, the US banking giant joined three other large US banks in reporting year-on-year profit increases that pointed to continued health in the US consumer.
JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum described US consumer spending as "sort of robust," adding that the consumer credit picture remains "quite resilient" despite persistent inflationary trends.
The strong bank earnings gave some support to Wall Street indices, although investors remained cautious ahead of Wednesday's consumer price index data, a key input to upcoming Federal Reserve decisions.
"Any real acceleration (in inflation) would probably send yields back up, the dollar back up, and that could be a problem for equities," said Peter Cardillo of Spartan Capital Securities.
The S&P 500 finished essentially flat, while both the Dow and Nasdaq ended modestly lower.
Earlier, Asian equity markets were under renewed pressure due to weakness in AI-related names.
The selling came after Hock Tan, chief executive of the US semiconductor giant Broadcom, likened the AI buying frenzy to gambling.
"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," Tan told a conference in Singapore, saying they "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
The International Monetary Fund weighed in on the debate, warning of an AI correction at the beginning of its annual meeting in Bangkok.
The boom in artificial intelligence -- and the related rush to manufacture semiconductors and build data centres -- has provided a boost to global growth despite geopolitical pressures including the Middle East war.
But "growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels... or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected", the IMF said in its Global Financial Stability Report.
On the trading floors, South Korea's Kospi index tanked 5.5 per cent by the close as chip titans SK hynix and Samsung took a beating.
The decline also followed reports that China's CXMT had made progress on new technology to boost memory chip density, which rival firms have also been racing to achieve.
The company is aiming to release a new server-memory product based on the structure by the end of the year, the reports said.
"The tech sector is taking it on the chin," said Trade Nation analyst David Morrison, noting that the CXMT development suggests that going forward, supplies of a key type of memory chips might not be as tight as many investors had thought.
Japanese stocks also slumped, with chipmaker Kioxia tumbling more than 13 per cent on the Nikkei 225, which lost 1.8 per cent.

Title: Oil prices settle mixed, focus on US-Russia diesel deal, Saudi Yemen attacks
Article:
LONDON/SINGAPORE: Oil prices were mixed on Tuesday as hopes the US-Russia diesel deal could free up more supplies from Moscow offset attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen that could result in additional supply disruptions.
Brent futures settled at US$105.69 per barrel, down 96 cents, or 0.9 per cent from Monday, which was its highest settlement since Sept 15.
US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 40 cents, or 0.4 per cent, to settle at US$94.14, the highest close for WTI since Sept 24.
WTI futures for calendar 2027 rose to a record high for a 12th day in a row, reaching US$84 per barrel. On Monday, Brent futures for calendar 2027 rose to a record high for a fourth day in a row, reaching US$90.
The Kremlin said it did not see any direct link between a deal on exporting Russian diesel to the US and Moscow's stance on the Ukraine peace talks.
It was commenting on a Reuters source-based story, which reported that US President Donald Trump's envoys had told Ukrainian officials on Friday that the deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of an attempt to draw Russia back into negotiations over a possible peace settlement in Ukraine.
Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, according to US energy data.
Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets have helped support oil prices since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Any deal to end the Russia-Ukraine war could allow Russia to export more energy.
Ukraine received no warning from Western partners before a Russian missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday.
Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence even as he pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Trump said Russian diesel was for the rest of the world, not the US. In a sign the market is uncertain about Trump's diesel deal with Russia, US diesel futures were trading up around five per cent on Tuesday.
Diesel prices rose to record highs in many parts of the world in recent weeks due to global supply disruptions linked to Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and Iran's attacks on Middle East energy infrastructure.
Elsewhere, the UK's domestic spy chief said on Tuesday that Russia and Iran were stepping up hybrid warfare campaigns in Britain.
MIDDLE EAST ATTACKS
Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.
Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport over the weekend, while tanker attacks were reported near the Strait of Hormuz.
Loud booms were heard in the vicinity of Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, six sources told Reuters.
Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi militants of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia, amid a widening regional conflict fuelled by the US war with Iran.
Despite ongoing disruptions of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war, however, oil producer group OPEC+ posted a sharp gain in production in September, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) said on Tuesday, driven by an increase from Saudi Arabia.
About 20 per cent of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. OPEC+ includes OPEC and allies like Russia.
OPEC also lowered its forecast for 2026 oil demand growth for a sixth straight month, and raised its forecast for next year, citing the need for the world to rebuild inventories depleted by the Iran war.

Title: Fed Governor Cook's lawyer denounces Trump's latest attempt to remove her
Article:
WASHINGTON: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer has questioned the objectivity of a White House probe into allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, according to a letter seen by Reuters on Tuesday, challenging President Donald Trump's latest attempt to remove her from her role.
Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year as he moves to exert more control over a central bank he says is refusing to lower interest rates for political reasons. Cook denies any wrongdoing and has sued to keep her job.
Earlier this month, Trump announced a fresh inquiry into Cook and the appointment of a three-person committee to hold a hearing. The president later told reporters he would proceed with her firing if the committee recommended it. Cook's lawyers have said a fair hearing would show there was no legal basis for firing her.
In Tuesday's letter, Cook's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, noted that one of the proposed committee members, White House economic policy adviser Kevin Hassett, had previously pressured Cook to take leave from her post and suggested Trump had "cause" to fire her.
"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence — with no explanation for why it was not previously produced — is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.
Lowell said Cook would not be able to attend a hearing on Nov 5, the date announced by the White House, because she would be fulfilling her duties in Europe "at financial and monetary policy meetings".
The earliest Cook could attend any hearing would be after the Fed's policy meeting scheduled for Dec 8-9, he wrote.
A Supreme Court ruling in Cook's case earlier this year barred Trump from firing a Fed governor at will, noting the need for the Fed to remain politically independent, both in fact and in appearance, to do its job.
But the ruling also laid out a path for a possible removal if a Fed official was given a fair chance to see the evidence of the allegations and refute them. The White House appears to be pursuing that path.
The Fed raised its policy rate in September and is expected to do so again at its final meeting of the year.

Title: When haze can cloud our judgment
Article:
MALAYSIANS should not have to become fire investigators to ask for cleaner air.
When smoke crosses borders, frustration is understandable. People want those responsible held accountable and assurance that the same ordeal will not return.
The difficulty is that a satisfying explanation is not always a sufficient one.
Naming a company, blaming a farmer or condemning an entire industry may settle an argument in the comments section. It does considerably less to settle the embers.
After a working life spent largely in plantations, I believe the debate needs to begin with a practical test: will our response help prevent the next fire?
That means examining how land is managed, how quickly danger is detected and whether people have the resources to respond.
Responsibility matters throughout. But identifying a culprit and understanding why a landscape keeps burning are related tasks, not interchangeable ones.
Consider the smaller farmer for whom burning is an inexpensive way to clear land.
A prohibition does not put a machine in the field or make credit affordable. Enforcement needs to come with workable alternatives, equipment and support.
Poverty cannot excuse every harmful practice. Equally, expecting compliance without considering its cost leaves a predictable gap between policy and reality.
Nor should the inquiry end at oil palm. Forestry concessions, other agricultural holdings and community land form part of the wider landscape.
For growers, deliberately burning productive palms makes no commercial sense. Effective prevention requires cooperation across it, including better peat and water management, early warnings, prompt field checks and adequate firefighting capacity.
The people providing that capacity deserve attention too. Government crews, estate employees, villagers, smallholders and volunteers all have a part.
Their work continues after the pictures stop circulating: replenishing water, maintaining firebreaks, checking embers and returning to places thought to be safe.
Acknowledging their effort grants nobody immunity from investigation. It simply recognises that a landscape under scrutiny may also contain people working hard to protect it.
Satellite monitoring is invaluable in directing attention to possible fires. The difficulty comes when an alert is treated as a completed investigation.
Heat detected inside a concession establishes a reason to investigate that location. It does not, on its own, establish the ignition point, who was responsible or whether failures in prevention or response contributed to the damage.
A fire may have started within the holding, crossed from adjacent land or re-emerged from smouldering peat. These possibilities need field evidence, not a preference for whichever explanation suits one's position.
Operators have obligations here. Anyone attributing a fire to neighbouring land should substantiate the claim. Anyone promising effective prevention should demonstrate how those arrangements performed under pressure.
A well-written policy is useful; a functioning response is rather more useful when vegetation is burning.
Prolonged dry weather makes that response harder by increasing flammability and reducing available water.
Peat may continue burning beneath the surface, with renewed flames appearing later. Fewer satellite detections therefore warrant caution before declaring success.
Such conditions help explain the challenge. They do not remove responsibility for deliberate burning or negligent management.
There is another complication: some operators are easier to scrutinise because their boundaries and commitments are public.
Less visible actors may attract less attention simply because information about them is harder to obtain.
The answer is wider scrutiny, not leniency for certified businesses.
Certification sets commitments against which performance should be judged; it neither proves innocence nor makes every fire within a boundary proof of guilt.
Public claims deserve equal scrutiny. Percentages need context: what was counted, excluded and over which period?
Companies and campaigners alike can select figures that are mathematically accurate yet misleading.
Anyone making claims that affect reputations, purchasing or regulation should explain their evidence and give corrections due prominence when findings change.
For Malaysians breathing polluted air, careful investigation may seem frustratingly slow. Yet establishing responsibility accurately makes accountability stronger and corrective action more effective.
Examine operators and regulators. Hear communities. Test industry explanations and campaign allegations. Act firmly on proven wrongdoing and correct unsupported accusations.
Judge progress by better prevention, fair accountability and fewer people breathing the same smoke again.
Cleaner air depends on getting the response right, not merely winning the argument. Every fire season produces enough heat; our public debate should bring more light.

Title: Malaysia seeks Euro tech, talent and jobs as FTA deal nears June 2027 target
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must turn European investments into a catalyst for technology transfer, skilled job creation and stronger local industries as it seeks to move up the global value chain amid intensifying US-China competition, economists said.
Achieving this will require more than attracting foreign capital, they said in response to Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani's remarks.
Johari said Malaysia wanted European investments to facilitate technology transfer, develop highly skilled talent and create better-paying jobs as the country moves into its next phase of economic development.
He said the emphasis was shifting towards the quality and long-term value of inbound investments, with the ultimate goal of moving beyond participation in global value chains to creating and capturing more value within them.
"Ultimately, our objective is to move beyond simply participating in global value chains to capturing and creating greater value within them," he said at European Union-Malaysia Business Day 2026: Selangor in Focus today.
Economists said stronger links between multinational companies and local suppliers, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), alongside targeted investment incentives and skills development, will be crucial to ensuring domestic businesses capture more value from foreign investments.
EU-Asean Business Council executive director Chris Humphrey said Malaysia could build on its existing attractiveness as a foreign direct investment (FDI)destination to draw more European companies into the country.
The recent announcement of a significant investment in semiconductor production by Nasdaq-listed NXP Semiconductors NV underscored Malaysia's appeal to international investors, he said.
However, sustaining that appeal and attracting more high-value activities would also depend on improving market access and giving businesses greater certainty to invest for the long term.
Humphrey said the swift conclusion of a high-quality, deep and comprehensive Malaysia-European Union free trade agreement (FTA) would be an important step towards achieving this.
"We have seen a steep increase in EU investments in Vietnam since the EU-Vietnam FTA was implemented, and given Malaysia's economic fundamentals, I would expect a similar pattern to emerge," he said.
A comprehensive agreement could boost business confidence by opening up new sectors, removing trade barriers and providing greater certainty for companies on both sides, he added.
While an FTA could help attract more European capital, Universiti Teknologi Mara senior lecturer Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said Malaysia would need complementary domestic policies to ensure those investments strengthened local capabilities.
He said investment incentives should be tied to measurable outcomes, including the employment of skilled local workers, development of domestic suppliers, workforce training and collaboration with Malaysian universities and research institutions.
The government should also strengthen technical and vocational education and training to ensure local talent could fill higher-skilled positions.
"Ultimately, the objective is to move Malaysian companies beyond basic assembly and subcontracting into engineering, product design, advanced manufacturing and innovation," he told Business Times.
Idham said the proposed Malaysia-EU FTA could help attract higher-quality investments by improving market access, reducing trade barriers and providing greater regulatory predictability.
However, an agreement alone would not guarantee technology transfer or meaningful benefits for local businesses.
Its effectiveness would depend on complementary measures, including stronger intellectual property protection, more efficient customs procedures, clearer investment regulations and better access to financing for SMEs seeking to meet European standards.
He said the government should also facilitate partnerships between European investors and local suppliers through supplier-development programmes, industry-academia collaboration and targeted skills training.
With effective implementation, the agreement could help Malaysian businesses enter European markets, diversify export destinations and move into higher-value activities.
"The key measure of success should not simply be the volume of European investment attracted, but how much domestic capability, skilled employment and long-term economic value Malaysia gains from it," he said.
Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research senior fellow Dr Azmi Hassan said the push for higher-value investments reflected a broader shift in Malaysia's investment strategy over the past decade.
Previously, Malaysia focused on attracting FDI by highlighting its political stability, safe investment environment and availability of low-cost labour. That approach was no longer sufficient as the country sought to compete for more sophisticated investments, he said.
Malaysia was now targeting high-technology investments in areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) and the green economy, with greater emphasis on technology transfer and developing a highly skilled local workforce.
Rather than competing on low labour costs, Malaysia needed to offer skilled talent and the expertise required to support higher-value activities, he said.
The country was also strengthening its infrastructure, including through the development of data centres, to support AI-related businesses and other technology-intensive investments.
Azmi said the ongoing negotiations for the Malaysia-EU FTA could further strengthen the country's appeal to European investors, particularly those in advanced technology, green technology and AI.
The agreement could deepen investment ties with Europe and encourage more companies to establish high-value operations in Malaysia, supporting the country's ambition to move beyond attracting capital towards building stronger domestic capabilities, he said.

Title: Prasarana ramps up efforts to improve LRT reliability
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Prasarana Malaysia Bhd is stepping up efforts to improve Light Rail Transit (LRT) reliability through round-the-clock maintenance, closer supplier engagement and the introduction of 26 new train sets for the Kelana Jaya Line.
The measures aim to address technical problems affecting train operations and improve the passenger experience.
Prasarana acting president and group chief executive officer Dr Prodyut Dutt acknowledged that the Kelana Jaya line had faced greater reliability challenges this year.
From January to August, the line recorded one incident for every 749km travelled, compared with one incident for every 1,066km during the same period last year.
"There is no denying the fact that we are having more incidents this year than we had last year. On the Kelana Jaya line, that represents a deterioration of about 30 per cent," he said.
[[nid:1554936]]
In contrast, the Ampang line and Monorail recorded performance improvements of 20 per cent and 80 per cent respectively.
Dutt said prioritising the Kelana Jaya line was crucial as it carried the highest passenger volume, at 290,000 people daily.
He said 90 per cent of disruptions on the line stemmed from rolling stock issues, with two-thirds triggered by the automated emergency braking safety system.
The system activates automatically when onboard tachometer sensors, which monitor train wheel speeds, detect discrepancies of more than five per cent. Cable wear and track vibrations can affect the sensors and contribute to these discrepancies.
Dutt said the issue was linked to the operating characteristics of the line's linear induction motor (LIM) system, which has been in service since 1998.
"The design characteristic of a LIM system is that the braking is naturally very hard. Overseas operators using the same system, such as in Vancouver, face the same issues with tachometers and emergency braking."
[[nid:1554935]]
However, Dutt said converting or replacing the LIM system entirely was not feasible as doing so would require the replacement of the power supply, signalling, trackwork and civil infrastructure. Prasarana, therefore, had to work within the system's existing design parameters.
On the condition of the fleet, he said the Kelana Jaya line operated 74 trains across three generations, including 26 first-generation four-car train sets that had been in service for more than 17 years.
An assessment found that overhauling trains aged 15 years would cost almost 90 per cent of the price of a new unit. This prompted Prasarana to order 26 new train sets worth more than RM1 billion from Chinese manufacturer CRRC Corporation Ltd.
The first new trains are scheduled to arrive in March 2029, with two sets expected to be delivered each month thereafter.
While the new fleet is expected to support long-term improvements, Dutt said Prasarana was also implementing interim measures and engineering interventions to stabilise operations before the trains arrived.
[[nid:1554934]]
"That is why we are aggressively implementing interim measures and engineering interventions to stabilise operations."
Prasarana has also worked with CRRC to refine the braking profile of the new trains during the final design review, aiming to ensure smoother deceleration and improve passenger comfort.
To ease the immediate strain, Prasarana has introduced round-the-clock maintenance operations across its depots and specialised workshops to inspect, service and repair train systems.
During a recent visit to its facilities, a first-hand look at the operations was provided, including intensive maintenance work in the electrical, door system and main repair workshops.
However, Dutt said global supply chain bottlenecks remained a challenge, with critical components such as tachometers facing lead times of eight to 12 months. This had prompted senior engineering teams to meet suppliers directly to expedite orders.
"Cost is not the issue because the government has been very supportive through government guarantees and approved five-year funding programmes. Our main challenge is the lead time for spare parts."
[[nid:1554933]]
He added that a major overhaul of the train bogies - the heavy undercarriage structures housing the wheels, suspension and braking systems - on the nine-year-old third-generation trains was scheduled to begin in June or July next year.
To minimise the impact of service disruptions on passengers, Prasarana is refining its contingency measures. These include turning trains back at selected locations to reduce congestion at key stations, isolating affected track sections, operating shuttle services and deploying feeder buses.
Dutt said passenger communication was also being strengthened through one-way WhatsApp broadcast alerts for registered users.
The presence of auxiliary police, station officers and Prasarana Troopers is also being increased on station platforms and in concourses to help manage passenger flow. Bernama

Title: Saudi says Houthi attacks sparked Aramco fire, wounded four in Riyadh
Article:
SANAA: Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that an attack on an Aramco building in the kingdom's east sparked a "limited fire", while debris from intercepted Houthi missiles wounded four people in the capital, Riyadh.
It came hours after the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted several missiles on Tuesday evening, including over Riyadh.
A Saudi energy ministry official said an administrative building belonging to oil giant Aramco in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday evening, resulting in a "limited fire" but "no casualties or fatalities".
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency said on Wednesday that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital, and that 15 homes were damaged.
Earlier on Tuesday, the coalition struck oil sites across western Yemen in response to the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
The strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways", coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.
A powerful explosion then rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying "the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat".
While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness told AFP he "saw a projectile cutting across the sky" above a mall, saying it left "a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion".
"People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.
After Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites in recent days, the coalition issued its first evacuation order in the Yemeni capital since the war flared in July, before attacking the Yemen Petroleum Company facility on Sanaa's outskirts.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression" had targeted the oil firm.
Renewed threats
A strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.
The Saudi cabinet vowed at a meeting earlier on Tuesday, led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, that it "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait to be threatened".
An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa, fearing shortages, rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.
The Houthis had earlier issued a new threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead, calling on citizens to avoid them.
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia. Most recently, France told its citizens to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.
Economic woes
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year, with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 per cent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional downturn due to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the resumption in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fighting to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea — Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organisation said on Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
'Behaving very badly'
The Riyadh airport attack had prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that "the Houthis are behaving very badly", accusing them of acting "probably at the behest of Iran".
"I'll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!" he wrote, referring to next month's midterm elections.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

Title: US targets network funneling IT earnings to North Korea
Article:
WASHINGTON: Federal prosecutors said on Tuesday that they had made two arrests and seized more than 180 computers in an effort to dismantle an alleged North Korean scheme to profit from remote IT work based in the US.
In a statement, the Department of Justice said it had searched "more than 40 suspected 'laptop farms' across Texas" that generated more than US$3 million for Pyongyang by deceiving US employers into hiring North Koreans.
Alongside the two Americans arrested in Ohio and Pennsylvania on money laundering and identity theft charges, authorities charged 14 others in Operation Lonestar Roundup, 10 of whom are based in China.
"North Korea's rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies," said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
Tuesday's announcement is the latest in a series of law enforcement actions targeting US-based laptop farms — facilities housing multiple computers used to generate illicit revenue for the North Korean government.
In April, two US nationals, Zhenxing Wang and Kejia Wang, were sentenced to 92 months and 108 months, respectively, for a "multi-year scheme that used the stolen identities of at least 80 US persons and generated more than US$5 million in illicit revenue" for the North Korean government.

Title: Transboundary haze: Jakarta mulls Malaysia's offer to help
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Indonesia is carefully assessing Malaysia's offer of firefighting assistance, with thick smoke limiting visibility and complicating plans for aerial operations, the Indonesian embassy here said.
The embassy said the Indonesian government was coordinating internally, with the National Disaster Management Agency leading efforts to determine what form of aid would be needed most.
"Indonesia welcomes and deeply appreciates Malaysia's kind offer of assistance in addressing the current forest and land fires in Indonesia.
"The offer is being given serious consideration. This takes careful assessment because conditions in the field are complex.
"Thick smoke over some fire areas limits visibility, which affects how far aerial operations can be optimised on any given day," it said in a written response to the New Straits Times.
On Sunday, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said Malaysia was awaiting Indonesia's response to its offer of assistance to put out forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, which have contributed to the transboundary haze crisis.
He said the offer was conveyed directly to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka during his recent visit to Jakarta.
The embassy said both countries wanted to resolve the situation as quickly as possible, while ensuring any assistance could be deployed effectively and that personnel's safety in the air and on the ground was protected.
"We remain in close communication with the Malaysian authorities on this matter," it said.
On Indonesia's efforts to contain the fires, the embassy said President Prabowo had chaired a limited cabinet meeting to accelerate the response, instructing authorities to optimise available resources and strengthen coordination among ministries, regional governments, the armed forces, police and local communities.
It said fires were burning on peatland, where flames could persist beneath the surface and reignite even after visible fires had been extinguished.

Title: Social media, disappearing messages fuel drug mule recruitment [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Drug syndicates are exploiting social media and messaging platforms to recruit couriers and using disappearing messages to erase their digital trail and make it harder for authorities to uncover evidence.
Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said the recruitment of drug mules had evolved beyond face-to-face approaches, with syndicates taking advantage of digital platforms to identify and communicate with potential couriers.
He said recruitment could be done through social media, messaging applications and personal contacts, as well as seemingly legitimate offers of employment or overseas travel.
Syndicates were also exploiting disappearing message features, he said.
"Such features can be used to erase conversations and potential evidence if a courier is arrested or investigated."
Hussein said the prospect of making quick money remains the drug syndicates' main tool to entice people into carrying drugs.
"Potential couriers can be offered financial rewards to transport luggage, parcels or other items locally or overseas.
"NCID investigations have encountered both willing couriers and people who claim they didn't know drugs were concealed in their luggage or packages."
He stressed that claims of ignorance would not automatically absolve a suspect.
Hussein said international syndicates could also exploit the relative ease with which Malaysians travel within the region when selecting couriers.
However, he said, nationality alone was not the deciding factor for syndicates when recruiting drug mules.
"Other considerations include the person's reliability, mobility and perceived risk of detection."

Title: International drug rings eyeing other airports as KLIA steps up scrutiny [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: International drug syndicates are shifting their attention to other Malaysian airports as enforcement intensifies at the Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA).
Syndicates are now targeting Bayan Lepas International Airport in Penang, Kota Kinabalu International Airport in Sabah and airports in Ipoh, Perak, and Miri, Sarawak.
Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said intelligence revealed that syndicates were looking for alternative routes.
"We have detected attempts to use alternative airports. When a route becomes more difficult to exploit, syndicates will try to find alternative routes.
"Based on NCID's intelligence, there are indications that syndicates have begun looking at other airports as alternatives following increased controls at KLIA," he said in an exclusive interview recently.
The shift comes amid a sharp increase in drug cases detected at KLIA.
Between January and July, 108 cases were detected, compared with 54 in the corresponding period last year, while the number of arrests more than doubled from 57 to 121.
Hussein said drug seizures at KLIA jumped to 1,353.41kg this year compared with 235.36kg in the same period last year.
"That is nearly a six-fold increase. This year's haul is worth about RM108.35 million," he said, adding that the rise in seizures should not be interpreted as a weakness in airport security.
He said the large scale detections and seizures reflected improved intelligence, surveillance and continuous enforcement.
He said NCID did not regard drug trafficking through airports solely as a KLIA problem.
"International air entry points are assessed according to their risk levels, travel patterns, intelligence and changes in syndicate modus operandi.
"We also consider the possibility that syndicates may test airports with lower passenger volumes or fewer international flights," he said, adding that traffickers did not always seek out the busiest airports.
He said their decisions could be based on perceived enforcement risks, security controls, flight schedules and opportunities to evade detection.
"That is why NCID does not depend on monitoring one airport alone and continuously adjusts its enforcement strategy based on intelligence developments."
The spotlight on drug trafficking through Malaysia's international airports intensified after a Malaysia Airlines pilot was arrested at Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on July 31 with about 25kg of drugs.
Indonesian authorities seized 70,114 capsules believed to contain ecstasy and methamphetamine, worth about RM45 million.
Investigations found that the drugs were believed to have been obtained in the Klang Valley.
The case prompted closer scrutiny of security and enforcement at international airports nationwide, amid concerns that syndicates could exploit aviation networks, airport procedures and drug couriers to move narcotics across borders.
Police have also arrested another pilot who acted as the moneyman, controlling the flow of cash between the drug syndicate and the other pilot.
He is being held under a 60-day detention order under the Dangerous Drugs (Special Preventive Measures) Act.
